▪ Gains were narrow: on a six-month basis, only under-35s and households earning $100,000+ saw confidence rise. Confidence improved “much more so for Republicans”

Israelis are voting today in what many on both sides call the most consequential election in the country’s history. It’s the first since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack and the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran that followed, and turnout is running at the fastest pace in nearly half a century, per Reuters.

The choice is stark. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader, is running on his record against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran, backed by an endorsement from President Trump, and says only he can keep the country safe. His main challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is campaigning on accountability for Oct. 7, per the FT. That includes a state inquiry that Netanyahu’s coalition has resisted, reversing parts of the judicial overhaul and ending the military-service exemption for ultra-Orthodox men. On security, though, the gap is narrower. Both oppose a Palestinian state, and Eisenkot has pledged to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza within 18 months, per the WSJ.

What the vote probably won’t deliver quickly is a government. Final polls had Eisenkot’s bloc at about 54 seats and Netanyahu’s coalition at about 50, both short of the 61 needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, with Arab and unaligned parties holding the rest, per the FT. Both camps have pledged not to rely on the Arab parties. The final count is expected by Friday, with official results on Nov. 4. President Isaac Herzog will then designate a candidate, who gets up to 42 days to build a coalition, per Al Jazeera. If that fails, the process can pass to another candidate and then to parliament before new elections are called. That sequence produced four inconclusive elections between 2019 and 2021. Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister throughout, leaving him free to act on his pledge to resume the war with Iran, Bloomberg notes. Herzog has said he’ll try to avoid a repeat, raising the prospect that he pushes for a national unity government, per the FT.

Prediction markets lean toward change: Polymarket bettors gave Eisenkot about a 60% chance of becoming prime minister and Netanyahu 27%. As Brazil showed on Sunday, though, they can be quite wrong.

I’ve mentioned in the Week Ahead some who have been relatively prescient about market moves the past couple of years, including Deutsche Bank, Citadel’s Scott Rubner, and Ed Yardeni. Another has been HSBC’s Max Kettner, who, like the others, has recently turned away from his “Max Bullish” call, downgrading global equities to a neutral rating.

Kettner on Monday cut global equities to tactically neutral from maximum overweight and moved developed-market government bonds all the way to overweight from maximum underweight, positions he had held since mid-March. He said bond underperformance has become stretched and that the market mood has swung from cheering records three weeks earlier to mourning the end of the AI trade. “Given the constant narrative bingo we just can’t have the same level of conviction any longer,” he wrote.

He flagged potential AI regulation if the Nov. 3 midterms produce a Democratic sweep and renewed Middle East tensions as the near-term risks, per Reuters. HSBC also cut gold to overweight and raised oil to an outright overweight, according to ZeroHedge. Kettner prefers the equal-weight S&P 500 over the Nasdaq 100, expects near-term dips to be buying opportunities, more so for equities than credit, and remains bullish into 2027.

This is a downgrade to “buy the dip,” not a bear call he said.

In terms of his track record, Kettner’s been more right than wrong the past few years. Bloomberg’s chart shows Kettner heavily overweight stocks for most of the past three years. In 2025, he cut U.S. stocks to neutral on March 10 and to underweight on March 25. The S&P 500 then fell about 14% to its April 8 low.  When he upgraded back to overweight on June 11, the index was about 4% above where he had gone underweight.

This year, he went maximum overweight in mid-March, a bit before the S&P 500 bottomed on March 30th after a 9.1% drop from its January high. He called the first proper buy signal since Liberation Day about a week after that low, and the index went on to gain 23.3% to the Oct. 6 record. His maximum underweight in sovereigns also paid off.

Despite all the headwinds, German business leaders are the most optimistic about the future since early 2022, and they’ve been pretty good forecasters of where things are headed boding well for the German economy.

▪ Business climate rose to 90.2 from 89.9, the highest since May 2023 and a sixth straight monthly gain
▪ Expectations rose to 91.6 from 90.4, the highest since February 2022
▪ Current situation slipped to 88.8 from 89.5
▪ Manufacturing climate turned positive (+1.2), the highest since April 2023

Since 2005, ifo expectations have led German real GDP growth by about two quarters, according to Claude’s analysis (correlation 0.71 excluding 2020–21, 0.58 across all quarters). The current-situation level, as you might expect, is more of a coincident indicator, moving with GDP rather than ahead of it.

And since 2022, German firms have been gloomier than the GDP data, arguing for an even stronger reading. Measured against the pre-pandemic relationship, growth has run about 3.5 percentage 
points above what the expectations level implied.

What has been more consistent is the year-over-year change in the business climate. It has tracked GDP growth two quarters ahead with a 0.84 correlation excluding 2020–21, and 0.74 since 2022. October’s climate is 2.3 points above last year’s fourth-quarter average. On that relationship, that lines up with German GDP growth of roughly 2% year over year in Q2 2027, versus 1.0% in Q2 2026.

2-Year Auction Sees Foreign Bid Ease but Record Domestic Demand

The first of this week’s three coupon (>1 year in maturity) Treasury auctions came today in $69 billion of 2-year notes, and while the end result was a bit soft, the mix of buyers stood out. Direct (domestic) bidders ended up with a record share after indirect bidders, a group that includes foreign buyers, fell to the lowest since November 2021.

The sale cleared at 4.708%, down from 4.787% in September, which was the highest since May 2024, and tailed (came in above expectations) by +0.3bps against a when-issued of 4.705%. That was the second straight tail, after +0.2bps in September, and compares with a 6-mth avg of a -0.2bps stop-through.

Looking at the rest of the metrics:

-Overall demand (bid/cover) fell to 2.59, the lowest since March, from 2.63 in September and below the 6-mth avg of 2.64.

-Indirect bidders (which include foreign buyers) dropped to 45.7%, the lowest since November 2021, from 57.8% in September and well below the six-month average of 58.3%.

-Direct (domestic) bidders jumped to 41.3%, the highest in Treasury data going back to 2008 (easily topping 38.2% in October 2012), from 29.0% in September and well above the six-month average of 30.4%.

-That left dealers (another metric of the strength of demand - the lower the better) with 13.0%, down from 13.2% in September but above the six-month average of 11.3%.

The indirect drop is worth watching and comes on the heels of my post this weekend about concerns that Japanese investors may be stepping back from Treasuries (link below). Indirect bidders also include US funds, though, so Treasury’s investor-class data for October, released with a lag, will show how much of the pullback was actually foreign.

@investingLive’s Greg Michalowski gave it a C−, calling it “a soft auction, although the small tail and modest miss in bid to cover keep it from being a particularly poor result he said.
